## Getting Started (November 16, 2026)

Jordan,

Your project started with a question about which world regions Ball State's geography courses covered, and why at those times. This workspace lets you experiment with another question that is sharper in two ways. First, it goes beyond geography: you will be looking at every course in the catalog, in any department, that names a world region in its title or description. Second, it goes beyond the curriculum: you will explore the *Ball State Daily News*, which shows what the campus was reading about the world while those courses were being planned. The question that can be asked from this experiment:

**When a part of the world appeared in the news at Ball State, did it also appear in what Ball State taught? How soon, and for how long?**

Your Historical Context already points to the significant moments to pay attention to: 1973 (the Arab-Israeli war and the oil embargo), 1979–80 (the Iranian Revolution and the Soviet invasion of Afghanistan), and 1989–91 (the fall of the Berlin Wall, the Gulf War, and the end of the Soviet Union). So I built this workspace to focus on **1970–1999**.

By the time you push this back to GitHub, you will have:

1.  **A headline dataset**: every headline listed for every regular issue of the *Daily News* from 1970 to 1999, about 110,000 headlines, with a check of how complete those lists are.
2.  **Region tags for the headlines**: the share of each year's headlines that names each world region.
3.  **Front pages around three turning points**, with the people, places, and nationalities a computer model finds on them (named entity recognition, as in Exercise 6).
4.  **A course dataset**: one row per course per catalog, in every department, with its title and description.
5.  **Region tags for the courses**, using the **same** region patterns as the headlines, so the two sources can be compared.
6.  **A side-by-side chart** of the news and the curriculum, region by region, over time.

Read the explanation before you run each chunk. The steps run in order, so each chunk needs the ones before it.

### Your sources

| Source | Where to get it | Where to put it |
|-------------------|---------------------------|---------------------------|
| Ball State University undergraduate catalogs, 1970–1998 | Downloaded by this workspace from The [BSU Course Catalogs collection](https://dmr.bsu.edu/digital/collection/BSUCoursCat) in the Digital Media Repository | `data/huneryager/catalogs/` |
| *Ball State Daily News*, 1970–1999 | Downloaded by this workspace from the [student newspaper collection](https://dmr.bsu.edu/digital/collection/BSUDlyNws) in the DMR | `data/huneryager/dailynews/` |

**Which catalogs?** Every undergraduate catalog from 1970 to 1998 that the DMR has: 15 editions, each covering two years (1970–72, 1972–74, and so on through 1998–2000). That includes all the editions published near your three turning points. The workspace uses the **undergraduate** catalog, not the graduate one, and skips supplements, class schedules, and evening or Saturday bulletins, which the DMR keeps in the same collection.

**Neither source needs downloading by hand.** The DMR runs on a system called CONTENTdm, which has an **API**: web addresses that return data instead of web pages. Section 3 uses it to download the headlines, Section 6 the front pages, and Section 8 the text of every catalog page. You used the same idea in our API exercise.

### What stays off GitHub

- **The catalogs' text** is large, and anyone can download it from the DMR. The `.gitignore` keeps `data/huneryager/catalogs/` off GitHub.
- **The newspaper text** is protected by copyright. The DMR lets you use it for research, but not republish it. The `.gitignore` keeps all of `data/huneryager/dailynews/` off GitHub: the headlines, the front pages, and the names found in them.

Remember not to edit the `.gitignore`.

Commit this `.qmd` file, the CSV files directly in `data/huneryager/` (your course and region datasets, your validation sheet, and the counts), and everything in `output/huneryager/`. Together they document your method, which is part of your Reproducibility grade.

## 1. One-time installation

You only need to run this chunk once. It is set to `eval: false` so it won't run every time you render the document. If you installed `nametagger` for Exercise 6, you already have it.

```{r}
#| label: install
#| eval: false

install.packages(c(
  "jsonlite",   # reading data from the DMR's API
  "readr",      # reading and writing text and CSV files
  "dplyr", "tidyr", "stringr",  # data wrangling
  "ggplot2",    # charts
  "tidytext",   # splitting text into words
  "nametagger"  # named entity recognition (Exercise 6)
))
```

## 2. Load packages and settings

If you're returning to this file at a later time, start here.

```{r}
#| label: setup

library(jsonlite)
library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(stringr)
library(ggplot2)
library(tidytext)

# ---- settings ----
datadir     <- "data/huneryager"                 # your datasets
catalog_dir <- file.path(datadir, "catalogs")    # the catalogs' text (not committed)
newsdir     <- file.path(datadir, "dailynews")   # the newspaper data (not committed)
outdir      <- "output/huneryager"               # your charts and writing

first_year <- 1970   # the years this project covers
last_year  <- 1999


# The three windows around your turning points, for the front pages (Section 6).
# Each runs over three school years.
windows <- tribble(
  ~window,     ~start,       ~end,
  "1972-75", "1972-08-15", "1975-06-15",
  "1978-81", "1978-08-15", "1981-06-15",
  "1989-92", "1989-08-15", "1992-06-15"
)

dir.create(newsdir, recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)
dir.create(outdir,  recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)
```

### Your regions

These patterns decide what counts as a mention of each region, in the headlines and in the courses. Using the same patterns on both sources is what makes them comparable. **They are your own categories** and reflect a decision you make here. Some notes on choices already made:

- Only country and region names, not adjectives like "French" or "Spanish," because those mostly name language courses. "Japan" also matches "Japanese," so language courses still show up for East Asia: decide whether they belong.
- `africa(?!n[ -]american)` means "africa, but not when it is the start of 'African American'," which is common in the 1990s headlines and is about the United States.
- `(?<!south)east asia` means "east asia, but not inside 'Southeast Asia'."
- `\\b` marks the edge of a word: `\\bindia\\b` finds "India" but not "Indiana."
- "International & global" catches words like "international," "foreign," and "world" (but not "World Series"). It's the broadest category: read its matches carefully.

```{r}
#| label: region-patterns

region_patterns <- c(
  "Western Europe"           = "europe|britain|england|france|germany|italy|spain|ireland|scandinavia",
  "Soviet Union & E. Europe" = "soviet|u\\.?s\\.?s\\.?r|russia|kremlin|moscow|eastern europe|east german|poland|polish|czech|hungar|romania|yugoslav|bosnia|serbia|baltic|lithuania|ukrain|berlin wall",
  "Middle East & N. Africa"  = "middle east|near east|mideast|israel|palestin|\\barab|iran|iraq|kuwait|saudi|egypt|leban|syria|libya|persian gulf|gulf war|opec|islam|muslim|moslem",
  "East Asia"                = "china|chinese|japan|korea|taiwan|hong kong|(?<!south)east asia|far east|\\borient(al)?\\b",
  "South & Southeast Asia"   = "\\bindia\\b|pakistan|afghan|bangladesh|vietnam|cambodia|laos|thailand|philippin|indonesia|southeast asia|south asia",
  "Africa"                   = "africa(?!n[ -]american)|nigeria|kenya|ethiopia|apartheid|rhodesia|zimbabwe|somalia|sudan|ghana|congo|zaire",
  "Latin America"            = "latin america|south america|central america|middle america|caribbean|mexic|cuba|nicaragua|salvador|panama|brazil|argentin|\\bchile\\b|grenada|haiti|guatemala|honduras",
  "Oceania"                  = "australia|new zealand|oceania|south pacific",
  "International & global"   = "international|global|foreign|\\bworld\\b(?! series)"
)

# The events your Historical Context discusses. They appear as dashed lines on the charts.
landmark_events <- tribble(
  ~year, ~event,
  1973,  "Arab-Israeli war, oil embargo",
  1979,  "Iranian Revolution; USSR in Afghanistan",
  1984,  "Guidelines for Geographic Education",
  1989,  "Berlin Wall falls",
  1991,  "Gulf War; end of the USSR"
)
```

# Part A: The world in the *Daily News*

## 3. Download the headlines

In the DMR, each issue of the *Daily News* has a description written by the library's catalogers, and that description is a list of the issue's **headlines**, separated by semicolons. The API can return the descriptions of 1,024 issues at a time, so a few requests download all thirty years.

Three small functions do the work:

- `dmr_url()` builds an API address. `URLencode()` turns characters like `^` into the codes a web address needs.
- `as_text()` handles empty fields. When a field is empty, the API sends `{}` instead of text, and this turns it into `NA`.
- `get_issues()` asks for one decade, 1,024 issues at a time, until it has them all.

```{r}
#| label: api-functions

dmr_url <- function(request) {
  URLencode(paste0("https://dmr.bsu.edu/digital/bl/dmwebservices/index.php?q=", request, "/json"))
}

as_text <- function(values) {
  if (is.character(values)) return(values)
  sapply(values, function(value) if (is.character(value) && length(value) == 1) value else NA_character_)
}

get_issues <- function(decade) {
  issues <- tibble()
  start  <- 1
  repeat {
    request <- paste0("dmQuery/BSUDlyNws/covera^", decade, "^all^and/title!descri/date/1024/", start, "/1/0/0/0/0/0")
    result  <- fromJSON(dmr_url(request))
    records <- result$records
    issues  <- bind_rows(issues, tibble(pointer   = records$pointer,
                                        title     = as_text(records$title),
                                        headlines = as_text(records$descri)))
    start <- start + 1024
    if (start > as.integer(result$pager$total)) break   
    # no more pages of results
    Sys.sleep(1)  # be polite to the DMR's server
  }
  issues
}
```

Now download the three decades. The result is saved, so this only runs again if you delete `data/huneryager/dailynews/issues.csv`.

```{r}
#| label: download-headlines

issues_file <- file.path(newsdir, "issues.csv")

if (!file.exists(issues_file)) {
  issues <- tibble()
  for (decade in c("1970s", "1980s", "1990s")) {
    message("Downloading the ", decade)
    issues <- bind_rows(issues, get_issues(decade))
  }
  write_csv(issues, issues_file)
}

issues <- read_csv(issues_file, show_col_types = FALSE)
nrow(issues)
```

The collection also holds supplements, weekend magazines, sports inserts, and class guides. Keep only the **regular issues**, whose titles include ", Vol." (for example, "1991-01-17 Ball State daily news, Vol. 70, No. 86"). Take the date from the start of the title, because the date field is sometimes empty.

```{r}
#| label: regular-issues

issues <- issues %>%
  filter(str_detect(title, ", Vol\\.")) %>%
  mutate(date = as.Date(str_sub(title, 1, 10)),
         year = as.integer(format(date, "%Y"))) %>%
  filter(year >= first_year, year <= last_year)

issues %>% count(year)
```

Split each issue's list into one row per headline:

```{r}
#| label: headlines

headlines <- issues %>%
  select(pointer, date, year, headlines) %>%
  separate_rows(headlines, sep = ";") %>%
  mutate(headline = str_squish(headlines)) %>%
  filter(!is.na(headline), headline != "") %>%
  select(pointer, date, year, headline)

nrow(headlines)
headlines %>% slice_sample(n = 15)
```

## 4. How complete are the headline lists?

The catalogers didn't list every story. In the 16 March 1970 issue, for example, every page is represented, but a few headlines are missing, and we don't know their rule. Before you count anything, find out what kind of story gets left out.

The chunk below picks three issues, one from each decade, and creates `data/huneryager/headline-validation.csv`. It only creates the sheet once, so your answers are never overwritten.

```{r}
#| label: validation-sample

set.seed(446)
validation_issues <- issues %>%
  mutate(decade = year %/% 10 * 10) %>%
  group_by(decade) %>%
  slice_sample(n = 1) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  mutate(link = paste0("https://dmr.bsu.edu/digital/collection/BSUDlyNws/id/", pointer),
         headlines_listed = str_count(headlines, ";") + 1)

validation_file <- file.path(datadir, "headline-validation.csv")

if (!file.exists(validation_file)) {
  validation_issues %>%
    transmute(date, link, headlines_listed,
              stories_in_issue = NA,   # fill in: how many stories the issue really has
              stories_missing  = NA,   # fill in: how many of them are not in the list
              what_is_missing  = "") %>%   # fill in: what kind? sports results, briefs, wire stories, world news?
    write_csv(validation_file)
}

validation_issues %>% select(date, link, headlines_listed)
```

### Check three issues

Open each link, go through the issue page by page, and count its stories. Fill in the last three columns of `data/huneryager/headline-validation.csv` and save it. Is any kind of story left out more than others in the DMR's description of each issue?

> The ones that are in smaller font tyoes.

## 5. Which regions make the headlines?

Check every headline against every region. A headline can name more than one region.

```{r}
#| label: headline-regions

headline_regions <- tibble()

for (region in names(region_patterns)) {
  pattern <- regex(region_patterns[[region]], ignore_case = TRUE)
  matches <- headlines %>%
    filter(str_detect(headline, pattern)) %>%
    mutate(region = region)
  headline_regions <- bind_rows(headline_regions, matches)
}

headline_regions %>% count(region, sort = TRUE)
```

**Read before you count.** List a sample of the headlines each region matched. Wrong matches mean a pattern needs changing (in Section 2), and then you run this section again.

```{r}
#| label: read-headline-matches

headline_regions %>%
  group_by(region) %>%
  slice_sample(n = 5) %>%
  select(region, headline, date)
```

The number of headlines listed per issue changes over time (about 25 in the early 1970s, about 16 in the late 1970s), so raw counts would mislead. Compare **shares**: the percentage of each year's headlines that name each region.

```{r}
#| label: headline-share

headlines_per_year <- headlines %>% count(year, name = "all_headlines")

news_share <- headline_regions %>%
  count(year, region) %>%
  complete(year, region, fill = list(n = 0)) %>%   # years with no matches get a 0, not a gap
  left_join(headlines_per_year, by = "year") %>%
  mutate(percent = round(100 * n / all_headlines, 2))

write_csv(news_share, file.path(datadir, "news-region-share.csv"))

news_share %>%
  filter(region != "International & global") %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = year, y = percent)) +
  geom_vline(data = landmark_events, aes(xintercept = year), linetype = "dashed", color = "grey60") +
  geom_line() +
  facet_wrap(~ region, ncol = 2) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(1970, 1980, 1990)) +
  labs(title = "World regions in Ball State Daily News headlines, 1970-1999",
       subtitle = "Percent of each year's listed headlines that name the region",
       x = NULL, y = "Percent of headlines") +
  theme_minimal()

ggsave(file.path(outdir, "headline-regions.png"), width = 9, height = 8)
```

These are small numbers: often fewer than a hundred headlines a region in a year. A jump in a single year may be one big story. Look for changes that last.

## 6. Front pages around the three turning points

Headlines are short. To see *how* the world was written about, you'll read whole front pages in your three windows. Each issue is made of separate pages, and each page has its own text from OCR (optical character recognition). Getting one front page takes two requests: one for the issue's list of pages, and one for the first page's text.

There are about 500 issues in each window. To keep the download to about half an hour, the chunk below takes **every other issue** (`every_nth <- 2`). Change it to 1 for every issue, or 3 for every third.

```{r}
#| label: window-issues

every_nth <- 2

window_issues <- tibble()
for (i in seq_len(nrow(windows))) {
  in_window <- issues %>%
    filter(date >= as.Date(windows$start[i]), date <= as.Date(windows$end[i])) %>%
    arrange(date) %>%
    filter((row_number() - 1) %% every_nth == 0) %>%   # keep every nth issue
    mutate(window = windows$window[i])
  window_issues <- bind_rows(window_issues, in_window)
}

window_issues %>% count(window)
```

This function downloads one issue's front page. If a request fails, it returns `NA` instead of stopping the whole loop:

```{r}
#| label: front-page-function

get_front_page <- function(pointer) {
  tryCatch({
    pages      <- fromJSON(dmr_url(paste0("dmGetCompoundObjectInfo/BSUDlyNws/", pointer)))
    first_page <- pages$page$pageptr[1]
    page_info  <- fromJSON(dmr_url(paste0("dmGetItemInfo/BSUDlyNws/", first_page)))
    as_text(list(page_info$full))
  }, error = function(e) NA_character_)
}
```

Now download the front pages. Each page is saved as its own text file, named by date, and the loop **skips pages it has already saved**. If the download stops (your laptop sleeps, the Wi-Fi drops), just run the chunk again, and it picks up where it left off.

```{r}
#| label: download-front-pages

frontpage_dir <- file.path(newsdir, "frontpages")
dir.create(frontpage_dir, showWarnings = FALSE)

for (i in seq_len(nrow(window_issues))) {
  page_file <- file.path(frontpage_dir, paste0(window_issues$date[i], "_", window_issues$pointer[i], ".txt"))
  if (file.exists(page_file)) next              # already downloaded
  text <- get_front_page(window_issues$pointer[i])
  if (!is.na(text)) write_file(text, page_file)
  if (i %% 25 == 0) message(i, " of ", nrow(window_issues))
  Sys.sleep(0.5)                                # be polite to the DMR's server
}

length(list.files(frontpage_dir))
```

Read the saved pages into a table. OCR breaks words at line ends ("frater-\nnity"), so rejoin them, then turn the line breaks into spaces.

```{r}
#| label: front-pages

front_pages <- tibble(file = list.files(frontpage_dir, full.names = TRUE)) %>%
  mutate(date    = as.Date(str_sub(basename(file), 1, 10)),
         pointer = as.integer(str_extract(basename(file), "(?<=_)\\d+")),
         text    = sapply(file, read_file),
         text    = str_replace_all(text, "(\\w)-\\n(\\w)", "\\1\\2"),
         text    = str_squish(text)) %>%
  left_join(window_issues %>% select(pointer, window), by = "pointer") %>%
  select(window, date, pointer, text)

front_pages %>% count(window)
```

Who wrote the front page? Stories from the wire services carry a dateline tag like "(AP)" or "(UPI)". Student reporters' stories carry a byline like "By TINA CARLIN." Flag both. A page can have both kinds, and the flags are rough, so read some pages to see how well they work.

```{r}
#| label: wire-or-staff

front_pages <- front_pages %>%
  mutate(has_wire  = str_detect(text, "\\((AP|UPI)\\)|Associated Press|United Press"),
         has_byline = str_detect(text, "\\bBy [A-Z][A-Za-z.]+ [A-Z][A-Za-z.]+"))

front_pages %>%
  group_by(window) %>%
  summarize(pages = n(),
            percent_with_wire   = round(100 * mean(has_wire)),
            percent_with_byline = round(100 * mean(has_byline)))
```

## 7. Names on the front pages

This is Exercise 6's model: it tags people (`PER`), places (`LOC`), organizations (`ORG`), and other names (`MISC`). For your question, `LOC` and `MISC` matter most: `MISC` holds nationalities and groups like "Soviet," "Iranian," and "Arab." The model was trained on English news from the 1990s, so it suits a newspaper, but expect mistakes from OCR errors.

This chunk prepares the text the way the model needs it (one word per line, capitals and punctuation kept) and loads the model you downloaded in Exercise 6.

```{r}
#| label: ner-setup

library(nametagger)

ner_input <- front_pages %>%
  transmute(doc_id = pointer, sentence_id = row_number(), text) %>%
  unnest_tokens(term, text, token = "words", to_lower = FALSE, strip_punct = FALSE) %>%
  group_by(doc_id, sentence_id) %>%
  summarize(text = str_c(term, collapse = "\n"), .groups = "drop")

model_dir  <- tools::R_user_dir("nametagger", which = "cache")
model_path <- file.path(model_dir, "english-conll-140408.ner")

if (!file.exists(model_path)) {
  dir.create(model_dir, recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)
  model <- nametagger_download_model("english-conll-140408", model_dir = model_dir)
} else {
  model <- nametagger_load_model(model_path)
}
```

`tags_to_names()` is the function from Exercise 6 that glues "New" and "York" back into one name. Running the model takes a few minutes, so the results are saved, and later runs read the saved file. **Delete `data/huneryager/dailynews/entities.csv` if you download more front pages and want to run the model again.**

```{r}
#| label: ner

tags_to_names <- function(tagged) {
  tagged %>%
    filter(entity != "O") %>%                       # keep only words inside a name
    mutate(type = str_remove(entity, "^[BI]-"),     # "B-LOC" -> "LOC"
           name_id = cumsum(str_starts(entity, "B-"))) %>%   # every B- starts a new name
    group_by(doc_id, sentence_id, name_id, type) %>%
    summarize(name = str_c(term, collapse = " "), .groups = "drop") %>%
    mutate(name = str_replace_all(name, "\\s+([.,;:])", "\\1")) %>%   # "St . Louis" -> "St. Louis"
    select(doc_id, type, name)
}

entities_file <- file.path(newsdir, "entities.csv")

if (!file.exists(entities_file)) {
  entities <- predict(model, ner_input) %>% tags_to_names()
  write_csv(entities, entities_file)
}

entities <- read_csv(entities_file, show_col_types = FALSE) %>%
  rename(pointer = doc_id) %>%
  left_join(front_pages %>% select(pointer, window), by = "pointer")

entities %>% count(type, sort = TRUE)
```

The most frequent places and nationalities in each window:

```{r}
#| label: top-names

entities %>%
  filter(type %in% c("LOC", "MISC")) %>%
  count(window, type, name, sort = TRUE) %>%
  group_by(window, type) %>%
  slice_head(n = 15) %>%
  arrange(window, type, desc(n))
```

Find two mistakes the model made (a place tagged as a person, an OCR error tagged as a name). Then look past Muncie and Indiana: which foreign places lead each window? Do they match the turning point, or something you didn't expect?

> Aids marked as MISC and AP as LOC. 1=None, 2=Israel, 3= Israeli, 4= Iran, 5= Iranian, 6= Soviet, 7= Iraq, 8= Iraqi, 9= German. I do think they match the turning point.

Now put the names into your regions, using the same patterns. Because the windows have different numbers of pages, count **names per 100 front pages**.

```{r}
#| label: name-regions

names_found <- entities %>% filter(type %in% c("LOC", "MISC"))
pages_per_window <- front_pages %>% count(window, name = "pages")

name_regions <- tibble()
for (region in names(region_patterns)) {
  pattern <- regex(region_patterns[[region]], ignore_case = TRUE)
  matches <- names_found %>%
    filter(str_detect(name, pattern)) %>%
    mutate(region = region)
  name_regions <- bind_rows(name_regions, matches)
}

front_page_regions <- name_regions %>%
  count(window, region) %>%
  left_join(pages_per_window, by = "window") %>%
  mutate(per_100_pages = round(100 * n / pages, 1))

write_csv(front_page_regions, file.path(datadir, "front-page-regions.csv"))

front_page_regions %>%
  select(window, region, per_100_pages) %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = window, values_from = per_100_pages)
```

# Part B: The world in the catalogs

## 8. Download the catalogs' text

The DMR's catalogs are stored like the newspaper: each catalog is an item made of pages, and each page has its own text from OCR. That text is already in reading order (the left column first, then the right), so you don't need the PDFs at all.

First, find the catalogs. The collection holds about 400 items, so the chunk keeps only the titles that follow the pattern of a main catalog, like "1980-1982 Ball State University bulletin and undergraduate course catalog". The regular editions cover **two** years, which leaves out a few one-year printings of the same catalog.

```{r}
#| label: find-catalogs

catalog_pattern <- "^(\\d{4})-(\\d{4}) Ball State University bulletin and (undergraduate )?course catalog$"

result <- fromJSON(dmr_url("dmQuery/BSUCoursCat/CISOSEARCHALL^catalog^all^and/title/title/1024/1/1/0/0/0/0/0"))

catalogs <- tibble(pointer = result$records$pointer,
                   title   = str_squish(as_text(result$records$title))) %>%
  mutate(first = as.integer(str_match(title, catalog_pattern)[, 2]),
         last  = as.integer(str_match(title, catalog_pattern)[, 3])) %>%
  filter(!is.na(first), last - first == 2,              # main two-year editions only
         first >= first_year, first <= last_year) %>%
  arrange(first) %>%
  rename(catalog_year = first)

catalogs %>% select(catalog_year, title, pointer)   # check: one row per edition
```

This function downloads the text of every page of one catalog. If a page fails, it gets `NA` instead of stopping the download:

```{r}
#| label: catalog-function

get_catalog_pages <- function(pointer) {
  pages <- fromJSON(dmr_url(paste0("dmGetCompoundObjectInfo/BSUCoursCat/", pointer)))$page
  text  <- character(nrow(pages))
  for (i in seq_len(nrow(pages))) {
    text[i] <- tryCatch({
      page_info <- fromJSON(dmr_url(paste0("dmGetItemInfo/BSUCoursCat/", pages$pageptr[i])))
      as_text(list(page_info$full))
    }, error = function(e) NA_character_)
    Sys.sleep(0.3)                     # be polite to the DMR's server
  }
  tibble(page = seq_len(nrow(pages)), text = text)
}
```

Now download them. A catalog has 300 to 450 pages, one request each, so each catalog takes a few minutes and all fifteen take about an hour. Each catalog is saved to its own file (`data/huneryager/catalogs/catalog-1970.csv`, and so on) as soon as it finishes, and the loop **skips catalogs it has already saved**. If the download stops, run the chunk again, and it picks up with the next catalog.

```{r}
#| label: download-catalogs

dir.create(catalog_dir, showWarnings = FALSE)

for (i in seq_len(nrow(catalogs))) {
  catalog_file <- file.path(catalog_dir, paste0("catalog-", catalogs$catalog_year[i], ".csv"))
  if (file.exists(catalog_file)) next                # already downloaded
  message("Downloading ", catalogs$title[i])
  get_catalog_pages(catalogs$pointer[i]) %>%
    mutate(catalog_year = catalogs$catalog_year[i]) %>%
    write_csv(catalog_file)
}

catalog_pages <- tibble()
for (catalog_file in list.files(catalog_dir, pattern = "^catalog-\\d{4}\\.csv$", full.names = TRUE)) {
  catalog_pages <- bind_rows(catalog_pages, read_csv(catalog_file, show_col_types = FALSE))
}
```

## 9. Check that the catalogs have text

Compare the number of pages in each catalog with the number of pages that gave you text. Some pages are blank or are only a picture, so a few empty pages are normal.

```{r}
#| label: text-check

catalog_pages %>%
  group_by(catalog_year) %>%
  summarize(pages           = n(),
            pages_with_text = sum(!is.na(text) & str_length(text) > 50),
            characters      = sum(str_length(text), na.rm = TRUE))
```

::: callout-warning
## If a catalog has little text

If `pages_with_text` is far below `pages`, either some requests failed or that catalog has no OCR text. Delete its file in `data/huneryager/catalogs/` and run Section 8 again. If it's still short, don't try to fix it yourself: tell me which catalog.
:::

Each page's text is one long piece. Split it into **lines**, and number the lines on each page, so the next section can find course entries and page headings:

```{r}
#| label: catalog-lines

catalog_lines <- catalog_pages %>%
  filter(!is.na(text)) %>%
  separate_rows(text, sep = "\n") %>%
  rename(line = text) %>%
  mutate(line = str_squish(line)) %>%
  filter(line != "") %>%
  group_by(catalog_year, page) %>%
  mutate(line_number = row_number()) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  arrange(catalog_year, page, line_number)

nrow(catalog_lines)
```

## 10. Split the catalogs into courses

Every department's section ends with its course descriptions, and they all follow the same format:

> 150 Global Geography. (3) A basic survey course emphasizing geographic facts and…

A **number**, a **title** ending in a period, the **credit hours** in parentheses, and then the **description**. That format is what lets you find courses in every department at once. Four steps get there.

**Step 1: Remove the running heads.** Each page repeats a heading at its top or bottom ("212 College of Sciences and Humanities," "Geography and Geology 119"), usually with the page number, and those lines land in the middle of course descriptions. The chunk finds the first and last line of each page, and removes the ones whose words (ignoring numbers) repeat on at least three pages.

```{r}
#| label: running-heads

catalog_lines <- catalog_lines %>%
  group_by(catalog_year, page) %>%
  mutate(at_edge = line_number == 1 | line_number == max(line_number)) %>%   # first or last line of the page
  ungroup() %>%
  mutate(words_only = str_squish(str_remove_all(line, "\\d")))

running_heads <- catalog_lines %>%
  filter(at_edge) %>%
  group_by(catalog_year, words_only) %>%
  summarize(pages = n_distinct(page), .groups = "drop") %>%
  filter(pages >= 3, words_only != "")

running_heads %>% arrange(catalog_year, desc(pages))   # read these: are they all headings?

catalog_lines <- catalog_lines %>%
  left_join(running_heads %>% mutate(is_head = TRUE), by = c("catalog_year", "words_only")) %>%
  filter(!(at_edge & is_head %in% TRUE),
         !str_detect(line, "^\\d{1,3}$")) %>%      # and lines that are only a page number
  select(catalog_year, page, line_number, line)
```

**Step 2: Find each department.** Each department's list of courses starts with a heading in capitals that ends with its code in parentheses, like `GEOGRAPHY (GEOG)` or `HISTORY (HIST)`. The `fill()` function copies each department's code down to every line until the next heading.

**Step 3: Split the lines into entries.** A new entry starts at every department heading and at every line that starts with a course number. `course_pattern` describes that start: an optional department code (two to five capital letters), a three-digit number (sometimes with a decimal, like 395.1), sometimes an older number in parentheses, like 382 (482), and then a title starting with a capital letter. `cumsum()` (cumulative sum) counts the starts as it goes, so every line gets the number of the entry it belongs to.

```{r}
#| label: entries

course_pattern  <- "^\\s*((?:[A-Z]{2,5})\\.?\\s*)?(\\d{3}(?:\\.\\d)?)(?:\\s*\\([^)]{1,12}\\))?\\.?\\*?\\s+(?=[A-Z])"
heading_pattern <- "^[A-Z][A-Z ,&'-]+\\(([A-Z]{2,5})\\)$"

entries <- catalog_lines %>%
  group_by(catalog_year) %>%
  mutate(department    = str_match(line, heading_pattern)[, 2],
         is_heading    = !is.na(department)) %>%
  fill(department, .direction = "down") %>%
  mutate(starts_entry = is_heading | str_detect(line, course_pattern),
         entry_id     = cumsum(starts_entry)) %>%
  group_by(catalog_year, entry_id) %>%
  summarize(department = first(department),
            page       = first(page),
            entry      = paste(line, collapse = " "),
            .groups = "drop") %>%
  # rejoin words the OCR split at a line end ("chem-istry"), but keep hyphens before a capital ("Arab-Israeli")
  mutate(entry = str_replace_all(entry, "([a-z])- ?([a-z])", "\\1\\2"))

nrow(entries)
```

**Step 4: Keep only real course descriptions.** Many entries that start with a number aren't course descriptions: requirement tables list courses by number and a short title ("150 Global Geog (3)"), with no period before the credits and no description. Splitting an entry into title, credits, and description only works for real descriptions, so entries where it fails are dropped. Courses numbered 500 and above are graduate courses, so they go too.

```{r}
#| label: courses

courses <- entries %>%
  filter(str_detect(entry, course_pattern)) %>%
  mutate(number = str_match(entry, course_pattern)[, 3],
         rest   = str_trim(str_remove(entry, course_pattern)),
         # title. (credits) description
         parts  = str_match(rest, "^(.{3,150}?)\\.\\s*\\(([^)]{1,12})\\)\\s*(.*)$"),
         title       = str_squish(parts[, 2]),
         credits     = str_squish(parts[, 3]),
         description = str_squish(parts[, 4])) %>%
  filter(!is.na(title), as.numeric(number) < 500) %>%
  select(catalog_year, department, number, title, credits, description, page)

write_csv(courses, file.path(datadir, "courses.csv"))

courses %>% count(catalog_year)
```

::: callout-tip
### spot-check

Pick one department in one catalog (geography is a good choice, since you know it from your Close Reading). Count its courses by hand in the catalog on the DMR website and compare:

`courses %>% filter(catalog_year == 1970, department == "GEOG")`

Then read 10 titles from other departments. Some titles will have OCR errors ("Euro pe") and a few will run into the description when the credit hours are printed further along. Note how often, so you can say how reliable the dataset is.
:::

## 11. Which regions do courses name?

Tag each course with the regions it names, using the same patterns as the headlines. The loop checks the **title** and the **description** separately: a course called "Introduction to the Middle East" is about the Middle East; a course that mentions it once in its description may not be.

```{r}
#| label: course-regions

course_regions <- tibble()

for (region in names(region_patterns)) {
  pattern <- regex(region_patterns[[region]], ignore_case = TRUE)
  matches <- courses %>%
    mutate(region         = region,
           in_title       = str_detect(title, pattern) %in% TRUE,
           in_description = str_detect(description, pattern) %in% TRUE) %>%
    filter(in_title | in_description) %>%
    select(catalog_year, department, number, title, region, in_title, in_description)
  course_regions <- bind_rows(course_regions, matches)
}

write_csv(course_regions, file.path(datadir, "course-regions.csv"))

course_regions %>% filter(in_title) %>% count(region, sort = TRUE)
```

Which departments teach about the world? Read these: are the language courses (Chinese, Japanese, Russian) the kind of evidence you want? If not, list their department codes in `skip_departments` and run the next chunk again.

```{r}
#| label: region-departments

skip_departments <- c("FL", "FR", "GER", "SP","RUS","LAT", "JAPAN" )   # for example c("CH", "JAPAN") to leave out language courses

course_regions %>%
  filter(in_title, !(department %in% skip_departments)) %>%
  count(region, department, sort = TRUE) %>%
  group_by(region) %>%
  slice_head(n = 4)
```

Now the share of each catalog's courses whose **title** names each region:

```{r}
#| label: course-share

courses_per_catalog <- courses %>%
  filter(!(department %in% skip_departments)) %>%
  count(catalog_year, name = "all_courses")

course_share <- course_regions %>%
  filter(in_title, !(department %in% skip_departments)) %>%
  count(catalog_year, region) %>%
  complete(catalog_year, region, fill = list(n = 0)) %>%   # catalogs with no matches get a 0
  left_join(courses_per_catalog, by = "catalog_year") %>%
  mutate(percent = round(100 * n / all_courses, 2))

write_csv(course_share, file.path(datadir, "course-region-share.csv"))

course_share %>%
  select(catalog_year, region, n) %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = catalog_year, values_from = n, values_fill = 0)
```

::: callout-tip
## Your turn

Change `in_title` to `in_description` in the chunk above and run it again. Which regions are *mentioned* in descriptions far more often than they get a course of their own? That's the difference between being mentioned and being taught.
> Africa is mentioned more in the description than the title. The difference between being mentioned and being taught is the difference between having a whole course on a topic and having one day of a course on a topic.
:::

# Part C: Did the curriculum follow the news?

## 12. The news and the curriculum, side by side

Put the two shares on one chart, region by region: the news in the top row, the course titles in the bottom row. Their scales are different (a few percent of headlines, a few percent of courses), so each row has its own y-axis. What you're comparing is **timing**: when each one rises, and when it falls.

```{r}
#| label: compare
#| fig-width: 11
#| fig-height: 5.5

compare_regions <- c("Middle East & N. Africa", "Soviet Union & E. Europe",
                     "East Asia", "Latin America", "Africa")

side_by_side <- bind_rows(
  news_share   %>% transmute(source = "Daily News headlines", year, region, percent),
  course_share %>% transmute(source = "Catalog course titles", year = catalog_year, region, percent)
) %>%
  filter(region %in% compare_regions) %>%
  mutate(source = factor(source, levels = c("Daily News headlines", "Catalog course titles")))   # news on top

ggplot(side_by_side, aes(x = year, y = percent)) +
  geom_vline(data = landmark_events, aes(xintercept = year), linetype = "dashed", color = "grey70") +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point(size = 1) +
  facet_grid(source ~ region, scales = "free_y") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(1970, 1980, 1990)) +
  labs(title = "World regions in the news and in the curriculum at Ball State, 1970-1999",
       x = NULL, y = "Percent") +
  theme_minimal()
```

Save the visualization:
```{r}
ggsave(file.path(outdir, "news-and-curriculum.png"), width = 11, height = 5.5)
```

Lines on a chart don't show cause. If a course appears a few years after a region fills the headlines, that's a question for your Historical Context sources (who proposed the course? was there a new faculty member, a new program, new funding?).

Look closely at one region and one turning point. For the Middle East around 1973, for example:

```{r}
#| label: one-region

focus_region <- "Middle East & N. Africa"

course_regions %>%
  filter(region == focus_region, in_title) %>%
  select(catalog_year, department, number, title) %>%
  arrange(title, catalog_year)

headline_regions %>%
  filter(region == focus_region, year >= 1972, year <= 1976) %>%
  select(date, headline)
```

## 13. Check your work

Before you use this data in your project, check:

- [x] **Headlines.** Every year from 1970 to 1999 has regular issues (Section 3).
- [x] **Validation.** You've checked three issues against their headline lists and filled in `headline-validation.csv` (Section 4).
- [x] **Regions.** You've read the headlines and courses tagged with each region and changed the patterns where they were wrong (Sections 5 and 11).
- [x] **Front pages.** Each window has front pages, and you've read a few to check the wire and byline flags (Section 6).
- [x] **Names.** You've found the model's mistakes and know how often they happen (Section 7).
- [x] **Text.** Every catalog has text on (almost) every page (Section 9).
- [x] **Courses.** For at least two catalogs, one department's courses match your hand count (Section 10).
- [x] **Commit.** This `.qmd` file, the CSV files directly in `data/huneryager/`, and everything in `output/huneryager/` are committed. `data/huneryager/catalogs/` and `data/huneryager/dailynews/` are not.

## Thinking like a historian about this pipeline

Every step here **transforms the sources**.

- **The headlines are a cataloger's list.** You are counting the headlines the library's catalogers chose to record, decades later. Your validation in Section 4 tells you how far to trust them.

- **A student paper isn't only students' writing.** Much of the world news in the *Daily News* came from the wire services. That's still what Ball State students read, but it isn't what they wrote. Your wire and byline flags are a first way to tell them apart.

- **A catalog is a plan, not a record of teaching.** Catalogs list what a department *could* offer. A course can stay in the catalog for years without being taught.

- **Who writes a catalog?** Faculty propose courses, and curriculum committees approve them. A new course on a region usually means a new faculty member, a new program, or new funding, so look for those in Edmonds and Geelhoed's history of BSU before you link a course to a world event. That process takes years, so a delay between the news and the curriculum is expected.

- **The model has a point of view too.** The NER model learned from Reuters news in the 1990s. It knows the names that mattered to that newsroom, and it may miss names that mattered in 1972.

- **Your regions are an argument.** "Middle East" and "Soviet Union & E. Europe" are your categories. Report your patterns, and test whether your findings hold when you change them.

## Exploratory Data Analysis

### Check the packaging

> **Peng:** Before opening the wrapped "present," shake the box: how many rows and columns are there? And do they match what you expected? ([Peng, "Check the packaging"](https://bookdown.org/rdpeng/exdata/exploratory-data-analysis-checklist.html#check-the-packaging))

```{r}
#| label: eda-packaging

nrow(issues)      # about 5,500 regular issues expected
nrow(headlines)   # about 110,000 headlines expected
nrow(courses)
n_distinct(courses$catalog_year)   # how many catalogs?
```

### Run `str()`

> **Peng:** `str()` shows the class of every column. Make sure numbers are numbers, dates are dates, and text is text. ([Peng, "Run str()"](https://bookdown.org/rdpeng/exdata/exploratory-data-analysis-checklist.html#run-str))

```{r}
#| label: eda-str

str(headlines)
str(courses)
```

`number` is text on purpose: course numbers are labels, not quantities. You'd never add two of them together. `date` should be a Date, not text: if it isn't, the charts by year won't work.

### Check your "n"s

> **Peng:** Count things, and compare the counts with *landmarks*: numbers you know should be true. If you expect 1,000 people and find 20, something's wrong. ([Peng, "Check your 'n's"](https://bookdown.org/rdpeng/exdata/exploratory-data-analysis-checklist.html#check-your-ns))

A daily paper comes out about 170 times in a school year, so a year with far fewer issues is a gap in the collection. Your landmarks for the courses are your hand counts from Section 10. Also look for course entries that are too short or too long: a very short description may be a broken entry, and a very long one may be two courses joined together.

```{r}
#| label: eda-ns-1

issues %>% count(year) %>% arrange(n) %>% head(5)   # the years with the fewest issues

headlines %>%
  count(pointer) %>%
  summarize(fewest = min(n), median = median(n), most = max(n))   # headlines per issue
```

```{r}
#| label: eda-ns-2

courses %>%
  mutate(description_words = str_count(description, "\\S+")) %>%
  arrange(desc(description_words)) %>%
  select(catalog_year, department, number, title, description_words) %>%
  head(5)
```

### A first experiment: what words are distinctive of each window?

Your region patterns count words you chose. **tf-idf** lets the headlines suggest words: it finds words that are frequent in one window's headlines but rare in the others. You met tf-idf in our text-analysis exercises.

```{r}
#| label: eda-tfidf
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 6

window_words <- tibble()

for (i in seq_len(nrow(windows))) {
  in_window <- headlines %>%
    filter(date >= as.Date(windows$start[i]), date <= as.Date(windows$end[i])) %>%
    mutate(window = windows$window[i])
  window_words <- bind_rows(window_words, in_window)
}

window_words %>%
  unnest_tokens(word, headline) %>%
  anti_join(stop_words, by = "word") %>%
  filter(!str_detect(word, "\\d"), str_length(word) >= 3) %>%
  count(window, word) %>%
  bind_tf_idf(word, window, n) %>%
  group_by(window) %>%
  slice_max(tf_idf, n = 12, with_ties = FALSE) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  mutate(word = reorder_within(word, tf_idf, window)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = tf_idf, y = word)) +
  geom_col(fill = "grey40") +
  scale_y_reordered() +
  facet_wrap(~ window, scales = "free_y") +
  labs(title = "Words most distinctive of each window's Daily News headlines",
       x = "tf-idf", y = NULL)
```


Which of these words point to the world beyond Indiana? Is any of them a place, a people, or an event your region patterns missed? Write down two or three ideas.
